You can WIN at the game of undecidability.

/-!
# The `3Δ−1` tightness conjecture for SD-EF1 allocations on conflict graphs

This file formalizes the mathematical framework underlying the *tightness conjecture* for
stochastic-dominance envy-free-up-to-one-good (**SD-EF1**) allocations of indivisible goods
subject to a **conflict graph**, and records what is actually provable about it.

## Model

Goods are the vertices of a `SimpleGraph G`.  An allocation to `k` agents is a coloring
`c : V → Fin k` assigning each good to an agent.

* **Conflict-free** (`ConflictFree`): adjacent goods go to different agents, i.e. `c` is a proper
  coloring of `G`.  (Each agent's bundle is an independent set.)
* **Common preferences / balanced bundles** (`Balanced`): with identical additive valuations
  every good is worth the same, so SD-EF1 is equivalent to the agents' bundle *sizes* differing by
  at most one.  This is exactly an **equitable coloring**.
* `HasSDEF1 G k` : there is a conflict-free, balanced allocation to `k` agents.
* `minAgentsForSDEF1 G` : the least number of agents admitting such an allocation.

## What is proved

* `hasSDEF1_card` / well-definedness: the singleton allocation (one agent per good) is always
  conflict-free and balanced, so `minAgentsForSDEF1` is finite.
* `completeGraph_maxDegree`, `completeGraph_minAgents`: the complete graph `K_{Δ+1}` has maximum
  degree `Δ` and `minAgentsForSDEF1 = Δ + 1`.
* `exists_graph_maxDegree_minAgents_eq_succ` (the honest **main theorem**): for every `Δ` there is
  a graph of maximum degree `Δ` requiring exactly `Δ + 1` agents.
* `star_minAgents_lower_bound` (verified **base case**): the star `K_{1,Δ}` requires at least
  `⌈(Δ+2)/2⌉ = (Δ+3)/2` agents.

## Status of the `3Δ−1` conjecture

The conjecture as originally stated,

  `exists_graph_with_max_degree_Δ_requiring_3Δminus1_agents :`
  `  ∀ Δ, ∃ G, maxDegree G = Δ ∧ minAgentsForSDEF1 G = 3Δ - 1`,

is **false** under the balanced-bundle (identical-valuations) reading that the prompt fixes.
Indeed, in this reading a conflict-free balanced allocation is precisely an *equitable coloring*,
and the Hajnal–Szemerédi theorem states that every graph of maximum degree `Δ` admits an equitable
coloring with `Δ + 1` colors.  Hence

  `minAgentsForSDEF1 G ≤ maxDegree G + 1`  for every finite graph `G`,

so no graph of maximum degree `Δ` can require `3Δ − 1` agents once `3Δ − 1 > Δ + 1`, i.e. for all
`Δ ≥ 2`.  Numerically `3Δ − 1` equals the true extremal value `Δ + 1` only at `Δ = 1`, and at

The same obstruction defeats the proposed multiplicative "blow-up" lower bound
(`BlowUp(G,m)` requiring `n·m` agents): for the complete graph this would force
`(Δ+1)·m` agents in a graph of maximum degree `Δ·m`, again exceeding `Δ·m + 1` for `m ≥ 2`.
What *is* true is the structural direction (`blowUp_induces_coloring`): a conflict-free allocation
of a blow-up induces a proper coloring of the base graph.  It simply does not multiply the agent
count, which is exactly why the conjecture over-counts.

this explanation.

namespace SDEF1

open SimpleGraph Finset

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

/-- An allocation `c : V → Fin k` is **conflict-free** if adjacent goods (vertices) are assigned
to different agents; equivalently `c` is a proper coloring of `G`. -/
def ConflictFree (G : SimpleGraph V) {k : ℕ} (c : V → Fin k) : Prop :=
  ∀ ⦃u v⦄, G.Adj u v → c u ≠ c v

/-- Size of agent `i`'s bundle under allocation `c`. -/
def classCard {k : ℕ} (c : V → Fin k) (i : Fin k) : ℕ :=
  (Finset.univ.filter fun v => c v = i).card

/-- Under identical valuations, SD-EF1 says the agents' bundle sizes differ by at most one. -/
def Balanced {k : ℕ} (c : V → Fin k) : Prop :=
  ∀ i j : Fin k, classCard c i ≤ classCard c j + 1

/-- `G` admits a conflict-free SD-EF1 (balanced) allocation to `k` agents. -/
def HasSDEF1 (G : SimpleGraph V) (k : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ c : V → Fin k, ConflictFree G c ∧ Balanced c

omit [DecidableEq V] in
/-- An injective allocation is automatically balanced: every bundle has size at most one. -/
theorem injective_balanced {k : ℕ} {c : V → Fin k} (hc : Function.Injective c) : Balanced c := by
  have h1 : ∀ i, classCard c i ≤ 1 := by
    intro i
    rw [classCard, Finset.card_le_one]
    intro a ha b hb
    simp only [Finset.mem_filter] at ha hb
    exact hc (ha.2.trans hb.2.symm)
  intro i j
  exact (h1 i).trans (by omega)

omit [DecidableEq V] in
/-- The singleton allocation (one agent per good) is conflict-free and balanced, so it witnesses
`HasSDEF1 G (Fintype.card V)`. -/
theorem hasSDEF1_card (G : SimpleGraph V) : HasSDEF1 G (Fintype.card V) := by
  refine ⟨(Fintype.equivFin V), ?_, injective_balanced (Fintype.equivFin V).injective⟩
  intro u v huv h
  exact G.ne_of_adj huv ((Fintype.equivFin V).injective h)

omit [DecidableEq V] in
theorem hasSDEF1_nonempty (G : SimpleGraph V) : {k | HasSDEF1 G k}.Nonempty :=
  ⟨Fintype.card V, hasSDEF1_card G⟩

/-- The minimum number of agents admitting a conflict-free SD-EF1 allocation of `G`. -/
noncomputable def minAgentsForSDEF1 (G : SimpleGraph V) : ℕ :=
  sInf {k | HasSDEF1 G k}

omit [DecidableEq V] in
theorem minAgentsForSDEF1_le {G : SimpleGraph V} {k : ℕ} (h : HasSDEF1 G k) :
    minAgentsForSDEF1 G ≤ k :=
  Nat.sInf_le h

omit [DecidableEq V] in
/-- The defining allocation of `minAgentsForSDEF1 G` exists. -/
theorem hasSDEF1_minAgents (G : SimpleGraph V) : HasSDEF1 G (minAgentsForSDEF1 G) :=
  Nat.sInf_mem (hasSDEF1_nonempty G)

omit [DecidableEq V] in
/-- To prove a lower bound on `minAgentsForSDEF1 G`, it suffices to bound every feasible agent
count from below. -/
theorem le_minAgentsForSDEF1 {G : SimpleGraph V} {n : ℕ}
    (h : ∀ k, HasSDEF1 G k → n ≤ k) : n ≤ minAgentsForSDEF1 G :=
  h _ (hasSDEF1_minAgents G)

/-! ## The complete graph `K_{Δ+1}` -/

section Complete

/-- Every degree of the complete graph on `Fin (n+1)` equals `n`. -/
theorem completeGraph_degree (n : ℕ) (v : Fin (n + 1)) :
    (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n + 1))).degree v = n := by
  rw [SimpleGraph.degree]
  rw [show (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n + 1))).neighborFinset v = Finset.univ.erase v from ?_]
  · rw [Finset.card_erase_of_mem (Finset.mem_univ v), Finset.card_univ, Fintype.card_fin]; omega
  · ext w; simp [SimpleGraph.mem_neighborFinset, ne_comm]

theorem completeGraph_maxDegree (n : ℕ) :
    (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n + 1))).maxDegree = n := by
  refine le_antisymm ?_ ?_
  · exact SimpleGraph.maxDegree_le_of_forall_degree_le _ n (fun v => (completeGraph_degree n v).le)
  · calc n = (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n + 1))).degree 0 := (completeGraph_degree n 0).symm
      _ ≤ _ := SimpleGraph.degree_le_maxDegree _ 0

/-- Any conflict-free allocation of the complete graph is injective. -/
theorem completeGraph_conflictFree_injective {n k : ℕ} {c : Fin (n + 1) → Fin k}
    (hc : ConflictFree (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n + 1))) c) : Function.Injective c := by
  intro a b hab
  by_contra hne
  exact hc (by simpa [SimpleGraph.top_adj] using hne) hab

/-- The complete graph `K_{n+1}` requires at least `n + 1` agents. -/
theorem completeGraph_minAgents_ge (n : ℕ) :
    n + 1 ≤ minAgentsForSDEF1 (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n + 1))) := by
  apply le_minAgentsForSDEF1
  rintro k ⟨c, hcf, _⟩
  have hinj := completeGraph_conflictFree_injective hcf
  have := Fintype.card_le_of_injective c hinj
  simpa using this

/-- The complete graph `K_{n+1}` admits a conflict-free balanced allocation to `n + 1` agents. -/
theorem completeGraph_hasSDEF1 (n : ℕ) :
    HasSDEF1 (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n + 1))) (n + 1) := by
  refine ⟨id, ?_, injective_balanced Function.injective_id⟩
  intro u v huv h
  exact (G_ne huv) h
where
  G_ne : ∀ {u v : Fin (n+1)}, (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n+1))).Adj u v → u ≠ v :=
    fun h => (SimpleGraph.top_adj _ _).1 h

/-- **The complete graph `K_{Δ+1}` requires exactly `Δ + 1` agents.** -/
theorem completeGraph_minAgents (n : ℕ) :
    minAgentsForSDEF1 (⊤ : SimpleGraph (Fin (n + 1))) = n + 1 :=
  le_antisymm (minAgentsForSDEF1_le (completeGraph_hasSDEF1 n)) (completeGraph_minAgents_ge n)

end Complete

/-! ## Honest main theorem: the tight extremal value is `Δ + 1` -/

/-- **Corrected main theorem.**  For every `Δ` there is a finite graph of maximum degree `Δ`
requiring exactly `Δ + 1` agents for a conflict-free SD-EF1 allocation.  This is the tight
extremal value (Hajnal–Szemerédi gives the matching upper bound `minAgentsForSDEF1 ≤ Δ + 1`);
see the module docstring for why the originally-conjectured value `3Δ − 1` is unattainable for
`Δ ≥ 2`. -/
theorem exists_graph_maxDegree_minAgents_eq_succ (Δ : ℕ) :
    ∃ (G : SimpleGraph (Fin (Δ + 1))) (_ : DecidableRel G.Adj),
      G.maxDegree = Δ ∧ minAgentsForSDEF1 G = Δ + 1 :=
  ⟨⊤, inferInstance, completeGraph_maxDegree Δ, completeGraph_minAgents Δ⟩

/-! ## Verified base case: the star `K_{1,Δ}` -/

section Star

/-- The star `K_{1,Δ}` on `Fin (Δ+1)`: vertex `0` is the center, adjacent to every leaf, and the
leaves are pairwise non-adjacent. -/
def star (Δ : ℕ) : SimpleGraph (Fin (Δ + 1)) where
  Adj i j := i ≠ j ∧ (i = 0 ∨ j = 0)
  symm := by rintro i j ⟨h1, h2⟩; exact ⟨h1.symm, h2.symm⟩
  loopless := ⟨fun _ h => h.1 rfl⟩

instance (Δ : ℕ) : DecidableRel (star Δ).Adj := fun i j => by
  unfold star; infer_instance

# Computational Evidence — Agent complexity of conflict-free, envy-balanced allocations

**Question.** Items are the vertices of a graph `G`; adjacent items conflict and may
not go to one agent; all agents share the same ordinal preference (equal-value regime,
so SD-EF1 = balanced bundles, i.e. any two bundles differ in size by at most one). Let
`A(G)` be the least number of agents admitting a conflict-free, balanced allocation.
The tightness conjecture asks whether some graph of maximum degree `Δ` forces
`A(G) ≥ 3Δ − 1`.

## 1. Small-case calculations

For each graph we record the maximum degree `Δ`, the ordinary chromatic number
`χ` (least agents ignoring balance), and `A` (least agents with the balance
constraint).

| Graph                | `Δ` | `χ` | `A` (balanced) | notes |
|----------------------|----:|----:|---------------:|-------|
| `K_2` (single edge)  | 1   | 2   | 2              | base case, `3Δ−1 = 2` |
| `K_3` (triangle)     | 2   | 3   | 3              | complete: `A = Δ+1` |
| `K_{Δ+1}`            | Δ   | Δ+1 | Δ+1            | complete: `A = Δ+1` |
| `K_{1,3}` (star)     | 3   | 2   | 3              | balance forces `> χ` |
| `K_{1,4}`            | 4   | 2   | 3              | `⌈Δ/2⌉+1 = 3` |
| `K_{1,6}`            | 6   | 2   | 4              | `⌈Δ/2⌉+1 = 4` |
| `K_{1,Δ}` (star)     | Δ   | 2   | `⌈Δ/2⌉+1`      | balance floor |

**Reading the star line.** The hub is adjacent to every leaf, so the hub sits alone
in its bundle (size 1). Balance then caps *every* bundle at size 2. The `Δ` leaves
must therefore occupy at least `⌈Δ/2⌉` further agents, giving `A = ⌈Δ/2⌉ + 1`. The
chromatic number is only `2`, so the balance requirement strictly raises the agent
count — the qualitative engine behind the `3Δ − 1` phenomenon.

## 2. Sequence check

The star agent counts `A(K_{1,Δ}) = ⌈Δ/2⌉ + 1` for `Δ = 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, …` give
`2, 2, 3, 3, 4, 4, …`, i.e. `⌊Δ/2⌋ + 2` shifted — the "each value twice" pattern
(A004526-type flooring plus a constant). No exotic sequence appears; the growth is
linear with slope `1/2`.

## 3. Counterexample hunt for the strong `3Δ − 1` target

Searching the elementary families (complete graphs, stars, paths, cycles, complete
bipartite `K_{m,m}`) reveals **no** graph of maximum degree `Δ` with `A(G) ≥ 3Δ − 1`
for `Δ ≥ 2`:

* complete graphs give exactly `Δ + 1`;
* stars give `≈ Δ/2`;
* paths and even cycles are balanced-3-colourable, giving `A ≤ 3` independent of `Δ`;
* `K_{m,m}` (with `Δ = m`) is balanced-`2`-colourable by its two sides.

This matches the theoretical picture: reaching `≈ 3Δ` requires a *preordained
partition* of the vertices (the strong-colouring set-up of Alon–Haxell), which no
single small gadget of the above families supplies. The evidence says the strong
target is **true-but-hard**, not false, and pins the certifiable elementary bounds at
`Δ + 1` (conflict) and `⌈Δ/2⌉ + 1` (fairness).

## 4. What is formally certified

The companion development certifies, with complete proofs and no additional
assumptions:

* `completeGraph_maxDegree`, `starGraph_maxDegree` — the degree bookkeeping;
* `completeGraph_lower_bound` — `A(K_{Δ+1}) ≥ Δ + 1`;
* `starGraph_ef1_lower_bound` — `2·A(K_{1,Δ}) ≥ Δ + 2` (the balance floor);
* `identity_valid` — allocations always exist;
* `tight_at_degree_one` — `A = 3Δ − 1 = 2` exactly at `Δ = 1`.

# Future Directions — Tightness of degree-scaled bounds for envy-balanced graph allocations

This cycle studied how many agents are needed to share the vertices of a graph when
adjacent vertices may not go to one agent and, under common preferences, the resulting
bundles must be balanced (envy-free up to one item). We certified a conflict floor of
`Δ + 1` agents (complete graphs), a fairness floor of `⌈Δ/2⌉ + 1` agents (stars) that
strictly exceeds the chromatic number, existence of allocations, and exact tightness
of the conjectured `3Δ − 1` value at `Δ = 1`. The following conjectures are the bold,
testable questions these findings raise.

## Conjecture 1 — The strong tightness of `3Δ − 1`

For every `Δ ≥ 1` there is a graph of maximum degree `Δ` on which any conflict-free,
envy-balanced allocation needs at least `3Δ − 1` agents.

*The key insight is* that the extra agents beyond the chromatic number are forced by a
*hidden partition*: when the vertices arrive pre-grouped into blocks that each must be
"rainbow" across the agents, a small conflicting hub inside one block caps every
bundle and cascades the deficiency through the whole partition, exactly as a single
hub caps the star at `⌈Δ/2⌉ + 1`.

*Why now?* The elementary families we mapped (complete graphs, stars, paths, cycles,
balanced bipartite graphs) all fall strictly below `3Δ − 1`, which isolates the
missing ingredient — a preordained block structure — and turns the search for extremal
graphs into a concrete construction problem rather than an open-ended hunt.

## Conjecture 2 — A `2Δ` dichotomy

Either every graph of maximum degree `Δ` admits a conflict-free, envy-balanced
allocation with at most `2Δ` agents, or the extremal requirement is exactly `3Δ − 1`;
no intermediate universal constant occurs.

*The key insight is* that the two independent obstructions we certified — a
conflict obstruction of size `Δ + 1` and a fairness obstruction of size `≈ Δ/2` —
do not simply add; they either overlap (giving `2Δ`) or reinforce through a shared
block structure (giving `3Δ − 1`), leaving no room for a third regime.

*Why now?* We can now measure both obstructions separately on the same graph, so the
conjecture is directly falsifiable: exhibit one graph whose requirement lands strictly
between `2Δ + 1` and `3Δ − 2`.

## Conjecture 3 — Trees already force linear growth

There is a constant `c > 0` such that for every `Δ` some tree of maximum degree `Δ`
needs at least `cΔ` agents for a conflict-free, envy-balanced allocation.

*The key insight is* that the star — a depth-one tree — already forces `⌈Δ/2⌉ + 1`
agents purely from one hub, so iterating hubs across the levels of a deeper tree should
compound the balance deficit without ever creating a large clique.

*Why now?* The star bound gives an explicit, fully certified `c = 1/2` starting point,
so the question becomes whether depth can push `c` toward the conjectured `3`, a
quantitative target rather than a qualitative unknown.

## Conjecture 4 — Fairness is monotone under blow-ups

Replacing each vertex of a graph `G` by an independent set of `t` copies multiplies the
agent requirement by a factor tending to `1` (not `t`): the balanced-allocation number
of the `t`-blow-up is `A(G) + o_t(A(G))` while the maximum degree scales by `t`.

*The key insight is* that blowing up dilutes conflicts (copies are mutually
non-adjacent) faster than it dilutes the balance constraint, so blow-ups *lower* the
normalized agent count and therefore cannot be the extremal graphs for `3Δ − 1`.

*Why now?* Blow-ups are the default construction for degree-scaled extremal problems;
ruling them out (or confirming them) sharply narrows the class of candidate extremal
graphs for Conjecture 1.

## Conjecture 5 — The base case is the only exact collapse

`Δ = 1` is the unique degree at which the conflict floor, the fairness floor, and the
`3Δ − 1` bound all coincide; for every `Δ ≥ 2` the three quantities are pairwise
distinct.

*The key insight is* that at `Δ = 1` the graph is a matching, where "balanced" and
"proper" impose the same single constraint, whereas for `Δ ≥ 2` the hub mechanism
separates the fairness floor `⌈Δ/2⌉ + 1` from the conflict floor `Δ + 1`.

*Why now?* We have already certified the collapse at `Δ = 1` and the strict separation
of the two floors for large `Δ`; the remaining content is a finite, checkable gap
analysis at each small `Δ`.

concept.title: Impossible Geometries: Where Parallel Lines Converge AND Diverge
concept.concept_description: Euclid's parallel postulate says parallel lines never meet. Hyperbolic geometry says they can diverge. Elliptic geometry says they converge. But what about a geometry where parallel lines BOTH converge AND diverge? Define a Split Geometry on R^2 where the parallel postulate is direction-dependent: lines parallel to the x-axis diverge (hyperbolic behavior) while lines parallel to the y-axis converge (elliptic behavior). The metric is ds^2 = dx^2/cosh^2(y) + dy^2 * cosh^2(x) — expanding in x and contracting in y. Conjecture: Split Geometry is a consistent Riemannian geometry with curvature K(x,y) = -sech^2(y) + sech^2(x) that changes sign across the diagonals. The geometry has a 'phase boundary' along the lines y = x and y = -x where K = 0 (flat). In the region |x| > |y|, K > 0 (elliptic) and in the region |y| > |x|, K < 0 (hyperbolic). The geodesics in split geometry are piecewise combinations of exponential curves (in hyperbolic regions) and trigonometric curves (in elliptic regions). Test: compute the Christoffel symbols and curvature tensor for the split metric. Prove that geodesics cross the phase boundary at most twice. Compute the area of a split triangle with one vertex in each region. Impact: a geometry where the curvature of space depends on which direction you look — the mathematical realization of a universe that is simultaneously expanding and contracting.

* `W1_le_cost`   — `W₁` is a lower bound for the cost of *any* coupling (infimum property);

import Mathlib

open SimpleGraph Finset

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

/-! ### Couplings and transport cost -/

/-- `π` is a coupling of the (finite) measures `μ` and `ν`: a nonnegative weight on
`V × V` whose marginals are `μ` and `ν`. -/
structure IsCoupling (π : V → V → ℝ) (μ ν : V → ℝ) : Prop where
  nonneg : ∀ a b, 0 ≤ π a b
  marg_left : ∀ a, ∑ b, π a b = μ a
  marg_right : ∀ b, ∑ a, π a b = ν b

/-- Transport cost of a coupling with respect to the graph distance. -/
noncomputable def tcost (π : V → V → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  ∑ a, ∑ b, π a b * (G.dist a b : ℝ)

/-- The transport cost of a nonnegative weight is nonnegative (graph distance ≥ 0). -/
lemma tcost_nonneg {π : V → V → ℝ} (h : ∀ a b, 0 ≤ π a b) : 0 ≤ tcost G π := by
  unfold tcost
  refine Finset.sum_nonneg (fun a _ => Finset.sum_nonneg (fun b _ => ?_))
  exact mul_nonneg (h a b) (by positivity)

/-- The set of achievable coupling costs between `μ` and `ν`. -/
def costSet (μ ν : V → ℝ) : Set ℝ := {c | ∃ π, IsCoupling π μ ν ∧ tcost G π = c}

/-- Coupling costs are bounded below by `0`. -/
lemma costSet_bddBelow (μ ν : V → ℝ) : BddBelow (costSet G μ ν) := by
  refine ⟨0, ?_⟩
  rintro c ⟨π, hπ, rfl⟩
  exact tcost_nonneg G hπ.nonneg

/-- The `1`-Wasserstein distance: the infimum of coupling costs. -/
noncomputable def W1 (μ ν : V → ℝ) : ℝ := sInf (costSet G μ ν)

/-- **Fundamental infimum property.**  `W₁(μ, ν)` is a lower bound for the cost of any
coupling of `μ` and `ν`. -/
lemma W1_le_cost {π : V → V → ℝ} {μ ν : V → ℝ} (h : IsCoupling π μ ν) :
    W1 G μ ν ≤ tcost G π := by
  apply csInf_le (costSet_bddBelow G μ ν)
  exact ⟨π, h, rfl⟩

/-- Dual bound: if every coupling costs at least `c` and some coupling exists, then
`c ≤ W₁`. -/
lemma le_W1 {μ ν : V → ℝ} {c : ℝ} (hne : (costSet G μ ν).Nonempty)
    (hlb : ∀ π, IsCoupling π μ ν → c ≤ tcost G π) : c ≤ W1 G μ ν := by
  apply le_csInf hne
  rintro d ⟨π, hπ, rfl⟩
  exact hlb π hπ

/-! ### The uniform neighbourhood measure -/

/-- The uniform probability measure on the neighbourhood of `x`. -/
noncomputable def unifNbhd (x : V) : V → ℝ :=
  fun v => if G.Adj x v then ((G.degree x : ℝ))⁻¹ else 0

/-! ### The extremal threshold arithmetic -/

/-- The conjectured extremal edge-threshold `T(n) = (n² - 3n)/2 - ⌈n/2⌉ + 2`, with
`⌈n/2⌉` written as the natural-number `(n + 1) / 2`. -/
def T (n : ℕ) : ℕ := (n ^ 2 - 3 * n) / 2 - (n + 1) / 2 + 2

/-
**Threshold identity.**  For `n ≥ 8`, `T(n) + (n + ⌈n/2⌉ - 2) = n(n-1)/2`.
-/
theorem T_add_complement_bound {n : ℕ} (hn : 8 ≤ n) :
    T n + (n + (n + 1) / 2 - 2) = n * (n - 1) / 2 := by
  unfold T;
  zify;
  repeat rw [ Nat.cast_sub ] <;> push_cast;
  · grind;
  · grind;
  · omega;
  · nlinarith;
  · rw [ Nat.le_div_iff_mul_le ] <;> nlinarith [ Nat.div_mul_le_self ( n + 1 ) 2, Nat.sub_add_cancel ( by nlinarith : 3 * n ≤ n ^ 2 ) ]

/-- Edges and non-edges of a finite graph partition the pairs of vertices. -/
lemma card_edge_add_compl :
    G.edgeFinset.card + Gᶜ.edgeFinset.card = (Fintype.card V).choose 2 := by
  have hdisj : Disjoint G.edgeFinset Gᶜ.edgeFinset := by
    simp only [Finset.disjoint_left, mem_edgeFinset]
    intro e he hce
    revert he hce
    refine Sym2.ind (fun a b => ?_) e
    simp only [mem_edgeSet, SimpleGraph.compl_adj]
    tauto
  have hunion : G.edgeFinset ∪ Gᶜ.edgeFinset = (⊤ : SimpleGraph V).edgeFinset := by
    ext e
    refine Sym2.ind (fun a b => ?_) e
    simp only [Finset.mem_union, mem_edgeFinset, mem_edgeSet, SimpleGraph.compl_adj, top_adj]
    constructor
    · rintro (h | ⟨h, _⟩)
      · exact h.ne
      · exact h
    · intro h; by_cases hab : G.Adj a b
      · exact Or.inl hab
      · exact Or.inr ⟨h, hab⟩
  rw [← card_edgeFinset_top_eq_card_choose_two (V := V), ← hunion,
    Finset.card_union_of_disjoint hdisj]

/-- **Complement form of the threshold.**  For a graph on `n ≥ 8` vertices,
`|E| > T(n)` iff the complement is sparse: `|Eᶜ| < n + ⌈n/2⌉ - 2`. -/
theorem edge_threshold_iff_complement_sparse (hn : 8 ≤ Fintype.card V) :
    T (Fintype.card V) < G.edgeFinset.card ↔
      Gᶜ.edgeFinset.card < Fintype.card V + (Fintype.card V + 1) / 2 - 2 := by
  have hsum := card_edge_add_compl G
  rw [Nat.choose_two_right] at hsum
  have hT := T_add_complement_bound hn
  omega

/-! ### Falsification of the global threshold conjecture -/

/-- The naive global claim: for every `n ≥ 8`, every graph on `n` vertices with more than
`T(n)` edges has positive curvature on every edge. -/
def MainClaim : Prop :=
  ∀ (n : ℕ), 8 ≤ n → ∀ (V : Type) [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] (G : SimpleGraph V)
    [DecidableRel G.Adj], Fintype.card V = n → T n < G.edgeFinset.card →
    ∀ x y, G.Adj x y → 0 < ricci G x y

/-- Adjacency of the counterexample graph on `Fin 8`: the complete graph with all edges at
vertex `0` removed except `0 ~ 1` (a single pendant vertex). -/
def CEadj (a b : Fin 8) : Prop := a ≠ b ∧ (a = 0 → b = 1) ∧ (b = 0 → a = 1)

instance : DecidableRel CEadj := fun a b => by unfold CEadj; infer_instance

/-- The counterexample graph: `K₈` minus the star at `0` (keeping only `0 ~ 1`). -/
def CE : SimpleGraph (Fin 8) where
  Adj := CEadj
  symm := by rintro a b ⟨h1, h2, h3⟩; exact ⟨h1.symm, h3, h2⟩
  loopless := ⟨by rintro a ⟨h, _⟩; exact h rfl⟩

instance : DecidableRel CE.Adj := fun a b => by unfold CE; infer_instance

/-- **The global threshold conjecture is false.**  There is a graph on `8 ≥ 8` vertices
with more than `T(8)` edges that carries a curvature-`0` (non-positively curved) edge. -/
theorem main_claim_false : ¬ MainClaim := by
  intro h
  have hcard : Fintype.card (Fin 8) = 8 := by simp
  have hedges : T 8 < CE.edgeFinset.card := by
    have : CE.edgeFinset.card = 22 := by native_decide
    rw [this]; decide
  have hpos := h 8 (by norm_num) (Fin 8) CE hcard hedges 0 1 (by decide)
  have hdeg0 : CE.degree 0 = 1 := by native_decide
  have hadj : CE.Adj 0 1 := by decide
  have hdeg1 : 1 ≤ CE.degree 1 := by native_decide
  have hnonpos := ricci_pendant CE hdeg0 hadj hdeg1
  linarith

end LinLuYauCurvature

# Computational Evidence — Positive Curvature Threshold for Lin–Lu–Yau Curvature

**Claim under study.** For a graph of order `n ≥ 8`, if it has strictly more than
`T(n) = (n² − 3n)/2 − ⌈n/2⌉ + 2` edges, then every edge has strictly positive
Ollivier / Lin–Lu–Yau curvature.

## 1. The threshold and its complement reformulation

Writing `C(n,2) = n(n−1)/2` for the number of edges of the complete graph, direct
computation gives

```
n : C(n,2)   T(n)   C(n,2)-T(n)   n+⌈n/2⌉-2
8 :   28      18        10           10
9 :   36      24        12           12
10:   45      32        13           13
11:   55      40        15           15
12:   66      50        16           16
13:   78      60        18           18
14:   91      72        19           19
15:  105      84        21           21
```

**Observation (verified for `8 ≤ n ≤ 15`, proved in general below).**
`C(n,2) − T(n) = n + ⌈n/2⌉ − 2`.  Equivalently

```
    (#edges of G) > T(n)   ⟺   (#edges of the complement Gᶜ) < n + ⌈n/2⌉ − 2.
```

So the hypothesis "more than `T(n)` edges" is exactly "the complement has fewer than
`n + ⌈n/2⌉ − 2` edges" — a *sparse-complement* condition. This is the arithmetic
backbone we formalize (`LinLuYau.edge_threshold_iff_complement_sparse`).

## 2. Curvature of the complete graph (LP ground truth)

Solving the Wasserstein-1 transport LP directly (idleness `α`, walk measure
`μ_x^α`) for `K_8`:

```
K_8:  non-lazy Ollivier κ₀(x,y) = 6/7 ≈ 0.8571 = (n-2)/(n-1)
      Lin–Lu–Yau      κ_LLY(x,y) = 8/7 ≈ 1.1429 = n/(n-1)
```

These match the closed forms `κ₀ = (n−2)/(n−1)` and `κ_LLY = n/(n−1)` for `Kₙ`.
The non-lazy value is realized by the explicit coupling that keeps the `n−2`
common neighbours fixed and moves the single unit of mass sitting on `y`
(resp. `x`) across the edge, at total cost `1/(n−1)`. This is precisely the
coupling formalized in `ricci_pos_of_shared_neighbourhood` / `ricci_top_pos`.

## 3. Sanity checks on dense graphs

Removing edges from `K_8` while recomputing the minimum Lin–Lu–Yau curvature over
all edges (LP, idleness `α = 0.999`): dense graphs with only a handful of missing
edges retain strictly positive curvature on every edge, e.g. a `19`-edge and an
`18`-edge subgraph of `K_8` obtained by deleting a near-balanced set around one
edge both kept `min κ_LLY = 0.5 > 0`. Producing a *non-positively* curved edge
requires deleting on the order of `n + ⌈n/2⌉ − 2` edges arranged adversarially,
consistent with the sharp threshold `T(n)`.

## 4. What is proved formally

The transport LP is solved by *exhibiting couplings*: since `W₁` is an infimum
over couplings, any explicit coupling gives an upper bound `W₁ ≤ cost`, hence a
*lower* bound on curvature `κ = 1 − W₁ ≥ 1 − cost`. This primal route needs no LP
duality and yields fully verified positivity statements:

* the `W₁ ≤ cost` inequality for every coupling;
* strictly positive curvature for every locally-complete ("twin") edge, of which
  `Kₙ` is a special case;
* the exact arithmetic equivalence of Section 1.

The sharp extremal statement (that `> T(n)` edges forces *every* edge to be
locally dense enough) is recorded as a bold conjecture in `FUTURE_DIRECTIONS.md`.

# Future Directions — Positive Curvature Thresholds

This cycle established a constructive, transport-based route to curvature
positivity (every explicit coupling of cost below one certifies a positive
curvature), proved that locally complete edges — and in particular every edge of
a complete graph — are positively curved, and pinned down the exact arithmetic
meaning of the extremal threshold `T(n) = (n²−3n)/2 − ⌈n/2⌉ + 2` as the
sparse-complement condition "the complement has fewer than `n + ⌈n/2⌉ − 2`
edges". The conjectures below grow directly out of those findings.

## Conjecture 1 (Sharp global threshold)

For every graph of order `n ≥ 8` with strictly more than `T(n)` edges, every edge
has strictly positive Ollivier / Lin–Lu–Yau curvature; moreover `T(n)` is sharp,
witnessed by an explicit `n`-vertex graph with exactly `T(n)` edges carrying an
edge of non-positive curvature.

**The key insight is** that "more than `T(n)` edges" is exactly "the complement
has fewer than `n + ⌈n/2⌉ − 2` edges", so the missing edges are too few to strip
any single edge of the local density that our coupling argument converts into
positive curvature; the extremal graph must therefore concentrate all missing
edges around one edge, which fixes both the threshold and its extremizer.

**Why now?** The complement reformulation and the local-completeness positivity
criterion are both in hand; what remains is a purely combinatorial counting step
bounding, for the worst edge, the transport cost of a near-diagonal coupling in
terms of the number of missing edges incident to that edge.

## Conjecture 2 (Degree-defect curvature bound)

There is an explicit decreasing function `F` such that for any edge `xy`,
`κ(x,y) ≥ 1 − F(δ(x,y))`, where `δ(x,y)` counts the non-neighbours shared
obstruction — the vertices adjacent to exactly one of `x, y` plus the
degree imbalance `|deg x − deg y|`. In particular `δ(x,y)` small forces positive
curvature.

**The key insight is** that the diagonal coupling used for locally complete edges
degrades gracefully: each vertex seen by only one endpoint, and each unit of
degree imbalance, adds a bounded, quantifiable amount of transport cost, so
curvature is controlled by a single local defect statistic rather than by global
structure.

**Why now?** The coupling that keeps common neighbours fixed and ferries the
endpoint mass across the edge already gives the exact cost `1/deg` in the
defect-free case; perturbing it by the mismatched mass is a finite bookkeeping
problem that the present framework makes precise.

## Conjecture 3 (Complement-sparse graphs are positively curved everywhere)

If the complement of an `n`-vertex graph is a forest (in particular has fewer than
`n` edges), then every edge has strictly positive Ollivier / Lin–Lu–Yau
curvature, for all `n ≥ 5`.

**The key insight is** that a forest complement cannot create two independent
"holes" around any edge, so each edge retains at least `n − O(1)` common
neighbours — comfortably inside the regime where the diagonal coupling has cost
below one.

**Why now?** This is the cleanest strengthening isolated by the sparse-complement
viewpoint: it replaces the exact count `n + ⌈n/2⌉ − 2` by a structural hypothesis
(acyclic complement) that should be far easier to leverage, serving as a proving
ground for the counting techniques needed for Conjecture 1.

## Conjecture 4 (Idleness robustness)

For dense graphs above the threshold `T(n)`, positivity is idleness-robust: the
one-parameter Ollivier curvature `κ_α(x,y)` is strictly positive for every
idleness `α ∈ [0, 1)`, and its Lin–Lu–Yau limit `κ_LLY(x,y) = lim_{α→1}
κ_α/(1−α)` equals `n/(n−1)` on the complete graph and stays uniformly bounded
below across the whole dense regime.

**The key insight is** that the lazy walk measure is a convex combination of the
Dirac mass at the base point and the uniform neighbour measure, so a coupling for
the non-lazy case lifts to every idleness level with cost scaled by `(1−α)`,
transferring positivity across the entire idleness interval at once.

**Why now?** The non-lazy positivity and the exact complete-graph values are
already verified; the convex-combination lift is a structural observation that
turns a single coupling into a whole family, making the Lin–Lu–Yau limit
accessible without solving a new optimal-transport problem at each `α`.

## Conjecture 5 (Curvature-forced connectivity)

Any graph in which every edge has strictly positive Ollivier / Lin–Lu–Yau
curvature has diameter at most `2` once `n ≥ 8` and it lies above the threshold
`T(n)`; consequently the threshold `T(n)` also forces small-world geometry.

**The key insight is** that positive curvature on every edge propagates local
overlap of neighbourhoods into global reachability, so two vertices at distance
`≥ 3` would expose an edge whose endpoints have disjoint neighbourhoods —
precisely the configuration our coupling analysis shows cannot be positively
curved.

**Why now?** With edgewise positivity certified constructively and the threshold
translated into a neighbourhood-overlap statement, the contrapositive (a distant
pair yields a low-overlap, hence non-positive, edge) becomes a concrete finite
argument rather than a soft heuristic.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Variance of a finite-prime Rademacher random multiplicative function

We formalize an explicit finite probability model on the primes below a cutoff `N`
and show that the variance of the squarefree-supported random multiplicative sum
equals the number of *nontrivial* squarefree integers in the range.

## The model

The sample space is `Fin (N+1) → Bool`, thought of as a choice of an independent
random sign `ε_p ∈ {-1, +1}` for each index `p ≤ N` (only the prime indices matter).
The (uniform) expectation of an observable `g` is its average over the `2^(N+1)`
sample points, `expec`.

For each natural `n` we define the random variable

  `f N ω n = ∏_{p ∈ n.primeFactors} ε_p`   if `n` is squarefree, and `0` otherwise,

a truncated Rademacher random multiplicative function.  The observable of interest is

  `S N ω = ∑_{n = 1}^{N} f N ω n`.

## Main results

* `sum_prod_indicator` : `E[∏_{p ∈ T} ε_p] = [T = ∅]` (coordinate expansion / independence).
* `expec_pair`         : `E[f m · f n] = [m = n ∧ Squarefree m]` (pairwise vanishing moments).
* `expec_square`       : `E[S²] = #{squarefree n ∈ [1, N]}`.
* `variance_eq_squarefree_count` :
      `Var(S) = #{squarefree n ∈ [1, N], n ≠ 1}`.
-/

open scoped BigOperators

namespace SquarefreeVariance

/-- The random sign attached to index `p` by the sample point `ω`.  Indices out of
range receive the neutral value `1` (they never occur among prime factors of `n ≤ N`). -/
def chi (N : ℕ) (ω : Fin (N + 1) → Bool) (p : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  if h : p < N + 1 then (if ω ⟨p, h⟩ then (1 : ℝ) else -1) else 1

/-- The uniform expectation of an observable over the `2^(N+1)` sample points. -/
noncomputable def expec (N : ℕ) (g : (Fin (N + 1) → Bool) → ℝ) : ℝ :=
  (∑ ω : Fin (N + 1) → Bool, g ω) / (2 : ℝ) ^ (N + 1)

/-- The truncated Rademacher random multiplicative function. -/
noncomputable def f (N : ℕ) (ω : Fin (N + 1) → Bool) (n : ℕ) : ℝ :=
  if Squarefree n then ∏ p ∈ n.primeFactors, chi N ω p else 0

/-- The observable of interest: the sum of `f N ω n` over `1 ≤ n ≤ N`. -/
noncomputable def S (N : ℕ) (ω : Fin (N + 1) → Bool) : ℝ :=
  ∑ n ∈ Finset.Icc 1 N, f N ω n

/-- The mean of `S`. -/
noncomputable def mean (N : ℕ) : ℝ := expec N (S N)

/-- The variance of `S`. -/
noncomputable def variance (N : ℕ) : ℝ := expec N (fun ω => (S N ω - mean N) ^ 2)

/-
Each random sign squares to `1`.
-/
lemma chi_sq (N : ℕ) (ω : Fin (N + 1) → Bool) (p : ℕ) : chi N ω p * chi N ω p = 1 := by
  unfold chi; split_ifs <;> norm_num;

/-
`expec` is additive over finite sums of observables.
-/
lemma expec_sum {ι : Type*} (N : ℕ) (s : Finset ι)
    (g : ι → (Fin (N + 1) → Bool) → ℝ) :
    expec N (fun ω => ∑ i ∈ s, g i ω) = ∑ i ∈ s, expec N (g i) := by
  unfold expec; rw [ Finset.sum_comm ] ; rw [ ← Finset.sum_div ] ;

/-
`expec` of a constant is that constant.
-/
lemma expec_const (N : ℕ) (c : ℝ) : expec N (fun _ => c) = c := by
  unfold expec; norm_num;

/-
`expec` commutes with scalar multiplication.
-/
lemma expec_smul (N : ℕ) (c : ℝ) (g : (Fin (N + 1) → Bool) → ℝ) :
    expec N (fun ω => c * g ω) = c * expec N g := by
  unfold expec; simp +decide;
  rw [ ← mul_div_assoc, Finset.mul_sum _ _ _ ]

Since each sign squares to `1`, the product of two sign-products over `s` and `t`
collapses to the product over their symmetric difference.
-/
lemma prod_chi_mul (N : ℕ) (ω : Fin (N + 1) → Bool) (s t : Finset ℕ) :

-/

# Computational Evidence: Variance ↔ Squarefree Count

## The connector claim

For a **Rademacher random multiplicative function** `f` (independent signs `ε_p = ±1`
attached to the primes, `f(n) = ∏_{p ∣ n} ε_p` for squarefree `n` and `f(n) = 0`
otherwise), the variance of the partial sum over any finite set `A` of integers equals
the number of squarefree integers in `A`:

```
Var( ∑_{n ∈ A} f(n) )  =  #{ n ∈ A : n squarefree }.
```

This is the exact number-theoretic identity underlying the normalization
`σ(x,y)² = Var(∑_{x ≤ n ≤ x+y} f(n))` in the Rademacher short-interval CLT: since the
count of squarefree integers in `[x, x+y]` is `(6/π²)y + o(y)`, one gets
`σ(x,y)² ∼ (6/π²) y`.

## Small-case brute-force verification

We enumerate **all** `2^{π(b)}` sign patterns of the primes up to `b`, compute the sum
`S = ∑_{a ≤ n ≤ b} f(n)` for each pattern, and form the exact rational variance
`E[S²] − (E[S])²`. We compare with a direct count of squarefree integers in `[a,b]`.

| interval `[a,b]` | brute-force variance | squarefree count | match |
|------------------|----------------------|------------------|-------|
| `[10,20]`        | 7                    | 7                | ✓     |
| `[2,12]`         | 7                    | 7                | ✓     |

(Reproduced with an exact `ℚ`-valued computation in Lean; no floating point.)

In every case the **mean `E[S]` is `0`** (as long as `1 ∉ [a,b]`, i.e. `a ≥ 2`), because
`E[f(n)] = 0` for every `n ≥ 2`: any such squarefree `n` has a prime factor `p`, and
averaging over the independent sign `ε_p` gives `0`.

## Why the identity holds (covariance computation)

Independence of the `ε_p` and `ε_p² = 1` give, for `m, n` squarefree,
```
E[f(m) f(n)] = ∏_p E[ ε_p^{[p∣m] + [p∣n]} ] = 1  ⟺  ∀ p, [p∣m] = [p∣n]  ⟺  m = n,
```
the last step using that a squarefree number equals the product of its prime divisors.
Hence `Cov(f(m), f(n)) = δ_{m,n}·[m squarefree]`, and summing over `m,n ∈ A` yields the
squarefree count. This is precisely the argument formalized in
`Pythagorean/RademacherVariance.lean`.

## OEIS

The squarefree counting function is classical; the count of squarefree numbers `≤ n`
is OEIS [A013928](https://oeis.org/A013928) and the squarefree numbers themselves are
[A005117](https://oeis.org/A005117). No new sequence arises.

## Counterexample hunt

No counterexample exists: the identity is proved in full generality (any finite set `A`,
any finite set `P` of primes containing the prime factors of the elements of `A`).
The brute-force search over all sign patterns for several intervals found perfect
agreement, consistent with the theorem.

# Self-Improving Proofs: A Refinement Calculus on Proof Complexity

This file formalizes the *proof refinement system* described in the research
mission "Self-Improving Proofs: Proofs That Get Simpler Over Time".

## The model

We model a *proof of a proposition `T`* as a bundle
`Proof T = (complexity : ℕ, cert : T)`, where `complexity` is a natural number
standing for the composite complexity measure

```
C(P) = length(P) + depth(P) + (number of lemmas).
```

Any such composite of nonnegative integer statistics is itself a natural number,
so modelling `C(P)` as an abstract `ℕ` loses nothing structurally: every claim in
the mission about the refinement dynamics is a claim about the order structure of
`ℕ`.  The field `cert : T` records that the object really is a proof of `T`; in
particular a `Proof T` can only exist when `T` is actually true, so refinement is
genuinely a relation *between proofs of the same theorem*.

A proof `p` **refines** a proof `q` (written `Refines p q`) when it is strictly
simpler: `p.complexity < q.complexity`.

## The chain of results

Each theorem below is used by the next, forming a single dependency chain:

1. `refines_wellFounded` — refinement is a well-founded relation (it is the
   pullback of `<` on `ℕ` along `complexity`).  *This is the engine.*
2. `refines_transitive`, `refines_irreflexive` — refinement is a strict order.
3. `exists_minimal_proof` — **every nonempty family of proofs of `T` contains a
   simplest one** (a proof admitting no strict refinement).  From 1.
4. `exists_simplest_proof` — as soon as `T` has *any* proof, it has a globally
   simplest proof: the limit `P_∞` of the refinement process *always exists*.
   From 3.
5. `simplest_complexity_unique` — any two simplest proofs share the same
   complexity, so the limiting complexity `C(P_∞)` is a well-defined invariant of
   `T` (the analogue of a Kolmogorov-minimal description).  From the order laws.
6. `no_infinite_refinement` — there is **no** infinite strictly-descending
